title: Wanting the Benefits, Resenting the Authority
author: Michael Foster
summary: Michael Foster argues that anyone who builds something well, whether a household, a business or a church, will eventually face an internal threat: people who want the benefits of what has been built without submitting to the authority that makes it possible. Drawing on a career of hiring and church planting, he uses Nehemiah as the model, noting that the rebuilt wall protected against outside enemies but could not keep out what insiders invited in. He gives examples across three settings, including teenagers who challenge their parents while enjoying the home, employees who resent the culture that produces their pay, and churchgoers who love the community but despise its pastor. His hiring heuristic, borrowed from Amazon recruiters, asks whether a candidate is more missionary than mercenary. He closes by insisting that authority must practice benevolent discipline, which means saying no, confronting entitlement and absorbing criticism, and that the cost of leadership is always lower than the cost of abdicating it.
points: Builders usually plan for external threats, but the more serious danger is often internal, from insiders who consume the benefits while resisting the authority behind them.
The missionary versus mercenary test separates people who care about a mission from people loyal only to pay or perks.
Nehemiah's story shows that walls cannot protect a community from compromise that insiders invite through relationships and divided loyalties.
The same pattern appears in households, companies and churches, so leaders in each need to defend the culture that produces the benefits.
Good authority requires benevolent discipline, including saying no and tolerating accusations of tyranny, because abdicating leadership costs far more.
quotes: I would summarize this threat as those who want the benefits of what’s been built and is being built without any regard for, or submission to, the authority that makes it possible.

The best companies hire, fire, and promote based on core values. They understand that even a wonderful product or service producing healthy profits won’t sustain a business that cannot attract and keep quality people.
The missionary cares about the mission of the business. He loves the space it’s in and the work it does. He doesn’t just want to benefit from it; he wants to contribute to it.
A mercenary, generally speaking, is primarily attracted to the benefits. He may think the mission is nice and be happy to contribute, but his loyalty is pay-to-play.

People come into a business wanting its benefits while deeply resenting the processes and practices that make those benefits possible. If that mindset isn’t corrected, they will undermine the very culture that produces what they came for.
The wall addressed an outside problem, but walls can’t keep out what the people inside invite in. Some of the gravest threats to Nehemiah’s work came from compromise within Jerusalem.
This is the cost of leadership. Sometimes it’s steep. But it is never as steep as the cost of abdicating God-given leadership.
